source.title: Tracing Multilingual Representations in LLMs with Cross-Layer Transcoders
source.authors: Abir Harrasse; Florent Draye; Punya Syon Pandey; Zhijing Jin; Bernhard Scholkopf

record.tranche_reason: The study measures multilinguality of Cross-Layer Transcoder features, not whether individual model neurons respond to unrelated inputs or have coherent jobs.
record.gate_note: The text reports layerwise multilingual entropy and cross-language feature overlap. These are adjacent findings about internal representations, but the study does not test neuron-level polysemanticity or whether the mixed inputs are unrelated. It does not report the cat/car neuron example.
record.test_reason: The study analyses Cross-Layer Transcoder features for multilinguality (language entropy, feature-set overlap, circuits, interventions) in GPT-2-style, TinyStories and LLaMA-3.2-1B models. It never measures whether individual MLP neurons respond to unrelated inputs, nor causes or measurement dependence of neuron polysemanticity. Zoom In is cited only as background on circuits. The one passing remark that early-layer CLT features also fire on 'unrelated tokens' (Appendix E) concerns transcoder features, not model neurons, and comes without a rate. 'cites_only' fits better than 'discusses': the paper does not discuss polysemanticity as a topic.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that models form shared multilingual representations in middle layers and decode language through a small set of high-frequency late-layer features, which can be intervened on to switch output language. They attribute non-English underperformance mainly to tokenization and weak downstream activations rather than missing circuits. They draw no conclusions about neuron polysemanticity.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Cross-Layer Transcoders and multilingual entropy/feature-overlap measurements, rather than the neuron visualization or interventions in the cited circuits work or the SoLU method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported entropy pattern varies with model depth: it is absent in the 4-layer TinyStories models, while the authors report it in GPT-2 and LLaMA-3.2-1B. The top-100 entropy measure is consistently lower than the score computed over a general training subset, especially in the earliest layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Layer-0 to layer-2 CLT features are mostly single-token, yet some also activate on unrelated tokens. The authors attribute this to a limited feature count (about 28K) across five languages. No rate is given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capacity-limited transcoder dictionaries trained on multilingual data yield some early-layer features that fire on unrelated tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: Middle-layer CLT features are more multilingual than early and late layers in 12-layer GPT-2 models and LLaMA-3.2-1B. The pattern is absent in 4-layer TinyStories models and persists without English in training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-shared transcoder features concentrate in middle layers of sufficiently deep language models.

fits_no_version.finding: The overlap of non-English language-specific CLT features with English-specific features rises from about 77% to 84% as the English share of training rises from 20% to 90%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training language proportions shape overlap among language-associated transcoder features.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The evidence concerns CLT features rather than individual MLP neurons and does not evaluate whether activations correspond to unrelated inputs. Several layerwise values are presented only in figures. The authors note that the 4-layer model lacks the reported pattern, that the LLaMA final-layer score may be affected by small activations, and that random-seed and implementation sensitivity were not exhaustively characterized.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. Other reported results, including output-language interventions and task-specific circuit analyses, do not measure neuron polysemanticity or the behavior described by the claim versions.

untested.parts: All: no MLP-neuron-level analysis of responses to unrelated tokens or contexts, and no per-layer share of such neurons.
All: no test of superposition as the cause of neuron polysemanticity.
All: activation function and architecture are not varied for polysemanticity.
All. The top-100 versus general-sample entropy comparison concerns the multilinguality of CLT features, not whether neurons count as polysemantic.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. The rows are faithful to the text, and all correctly link to no version.

versions.untested_parts: Image-classifier neurons and the InceptionV1 example.
Whether MLP neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, and the share of such neurons by layer.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by sparse features being packed under capacity pressure.
Whether initialization, regularization, or training noise causes polysemantic neurons when capacity is sufficient.
Effects of activation functions, architecture, or regularization on neuron polysemanticity and performance.
Whether apparent polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related jobs rather than unrelated inputs.
Whether neuron polysemanticity depends on activation range or explanation scoring.

rows.subject: GPT-2 models (four English-proportion mixtures; aggregate result)
rows.operation_detail: Measured activation-rate-weighted multilingual entropy of CLT features across layers using the top-100 score.
rows.measure: Average activation-rate-weighted multilingual feature entropy across layers
rows.value: Figure only; text describes relatively low entropy in early layers, a rise in middle layers, and a decrease toward output layers, robust across mixtures.
rows.note: This measures cross-language activation distributions of CLT features, not neuron responses to unrelated inputs.
rows.check: Entropy is computed over CLT features across languages, not over model neurons across unrelated inputs. The link to none is correct.

rows.subject: Multilingual TinyStories models (four English-proportion mixtures; aggregate result)
rows.value: Figure only; text says the rise-and-fall pattern is absent and all layers have similar entropy scores.
rows.note: The paper attributes the difference to model depth; this is a CLT feature-entropy result, not a neuron-polysemanticity result.
rows.check: Same as R1: a CLT feature-entropy result. The link to none is correct.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3.2-1B
rows.operation_detail: Measured general multilingual feature entropy across layers using CLTs.
rows.measure: General multilingual feature entropy across layers
rows.value: Figure only; text says the well-defined layerwise pattern is observed, with the final-layer jump potentially due to training dynamics.
rows.note: The appendix cautions that small-valued last-layer feature activations affect the multilingual score.
rows.check: Same as R1. The LLaMA CLT uses expansion factor about 4, unlike the other models; the row does not note this.

rows.subject: GPT-2 trained on balanced non-English data
rows.operation_detail: Measured activation-rate-weighted multilingual entropy across layers.

conditions.value: 25% French, 25% German, 25% Arabic, 25% Chinese; no English

rows.value: Figure only; text describes the characteristic rise-and-fall pattern as identical to that in English-dominant models, with peak entropy in layers 5–6.
rows.note: This result concerns multilingual CLT feature structure, not unrelated inputs to individual neurons.
rows.check: A CLT feature-entropy result for the no-English GPT-2. The link to none is correct.

rows.subject: GPT-2 models (20%, 50%, 70%, 90% English checkpoints; aggregate result)
rows.operation_detail: Computed overlap between non-English language-specific CLT features and English-specific CLT features.
rows.measure: Percentage of each non-English language's language-specific features overlapping English-specific features
rows.value: Approximately 77% at 20% English and 84% at 90% English; text says overlap increases across checkpoints.
rows.note: The statistic is overlap between sets of language-specific CLT features, not a measure of neuron polysemanticity.
rows.check: Overlap of language-specific CLT feature sets. This is not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: GPT-2 models (20%, 50%, 70%, 90% English checkpoints; aggregate result)
rows.operation_detail: Computed pairwise overlap among non-English language-specific CLT features.
rows.measure: Pairwise overlap among non-English language-specific feature sets
rows.value: Average 89% at 20% English; at 90% English, the gap relative to English overlap is described as reaching near parity.
rows.note: This compares feature-set overlap across languages; it does not establish that features respond to unrelated inputs.
rows.check: Overlap of language-specific CLT feature sets. This is not neuron polysemanticity.
